title: Emergency Communication, Incident Reporting, Documentation & Escalation

questions.q: The first step in the emergency communication flow is that the person at the site:
options: Declares the emergency to Operations Control Centre (OCC) with identity, location and nature in one clear message
Waits for Operations Control Centre (OCC) to discover the problem
questions.explain: Raise it first: one clear message — who you are, where you are, what has happened. Operations Control Centre (OCC) cannot act on what it does not know.

questions.q: After Operations Control Centre (OCC) acknowledges an emergency, its immediate actions include:
options: Only noting it in the log
Protecting the area — stopping movements, cutting power if needed — and dispatching help
Asking the site to manage alone
questions.explain: Acknowledge and act: protect the area first, then send help. Protection stops the incident from growing.

questions.q: At Escalation Level 1, charge of the incident passes to:
questions.explain: Level 1: the duty officer/Chief Controller takes charge and all points act on his instructions — one commander, no confusion.

questions.q: Escalation Level 2 is reached when:
options: Senior management is informed and external agencies — police, fire, hospitals, district administration — are engaged
questions.explain: Level 2 brings in senior management and outside agencies through laid-down contacts, when the incident exceeds railway resources.

questions.q: An emergency can be declared closed (stood down) only by:
options: The site staff who raised it
Operations Control Centre (OCC), after certification that the situation is safe/normal
questions.explain: Only Operations Control Centre (OCC) declares stand-down, after proper certification. Local staff cannot close an emergency on their own.

questions.q: After stand-down, logs and recordings of the incident must be:
questions.explain: Logs and recordings are evidence. They are preserved exactly as made, for the enquiry that follows.

questions.q: A written incident report should be:
options: Written in general terms without times
Completed a week later from memory
Full of opinions about who is at fault
Factual, timed and sequential — facts only, no blame language
questions.explain: A report answers what, where, when, who, what was done and what is pending — facts only. Blame belongs to the enquiry, not the report.

questions.q: The saying 'if it is not written, it did not happen' means:
options: Undocumented actions cannot be proved, checked or learned from — documentation is part of the work itself
questions.explain: In operations, the record is the proof. Good documentation protects staff and helps the system learn.

questions.q: Log entries must be made:
options: At the time of the event; late entries are marked as late, never silently back-timed
At the end of the week
questions.explain: Logs are completed at the time. A late entry is honestly marked late — back-timing a log is falsification.

questions.q: If a log entry contains an error, the correct way to fix it is:
options: Overwrite it so it looks original
Add a fresh, timed correction entry, leaving the original readable
questions.explain: A log is a legal record. Corrections are new entries; the original stays readable. Overwriting is treated as tampering.

questions.q: Times written in incident records should come from:
questions.explain: Use the system clock so that logs, recordings and event data all match on one timeline during the enquiry.

questions.q: The master record of an incident in the control organisation is:
options: The Operations Control Centre (OCC)/control log with time-stamped entries and recordings
questions.explain: Enquiries run on the Operations Control Centre (OCC) log and recordings. Everything else is secondary.

questions.q: The normal reporting chain for an incident is:
options: Site → Operations Control Centre (OCC) immediately by voice, with the written report following within the prescribed time
Written report first, voice call next week
questions.explain: Voice first, immediately — protection cannot wait for paperwork. The written report follows within the prescribed time.

questions.q: Evidence to be preserved after an incident includes:
options: Recordings, logs, Closed-Circuit Television (CCTV) and event recorder data
questions.explain: Preserve recordings, logs, Closed-Circuit Television (CCTV) and event recorders together — together they reconstruct the incident truthfully.

questions.q: Escalation, in simple words, means:
options: Hiding a problem till it solves itself
Passing the matter to the next higher authority, with full facts, when it exceeds your powers or resources
questions.explain: Escalate early with full facts. A small incident reported late becomes a big incident.

questions.q: A station controller realises an incident needs resources beyond his station. The best action is:
options: Struggle silently to avoid looking weak
Escalate immediately to Operations Control Centre (OCC) with the facts and the help needed
Wait for the next shift to decide
questions.explain: Escalation is a strength, not a weakness. Early escalation brings resources while they can still change the outcome.

questions.q: During an emergency, passenger announcements must avoid:
options: Expected time of the next update
questions.explain: Announce facts and actions being taken. Causes and blame are for the enquiry — speculation creates panic and rumours.

questions.q: A crew member notices a small lineside fire and informs Operations Control Centre (OCC), which arranges fire help. The crew's next documentation duty is:
options: Nothing — a voice call is enough
Ensure the event is entered in the log/report factually with times
Write the report only if the fire spreads
questions.explain: Voice action first, but the record must follow: what, where, when, who, action taken. Undocumented incidents cannot be reviewed.

questions.q: An officer asks you to quietly change a time in the incident log to 'make it look better'. You should:
options: Refuse — log entries are never altered; corrections go in as fresh entries
Change it but tell no one
questions.explain: Altering a log is tampering with a legal record, whoever asks. The honest route is a fresh correction entry.

questions.q: Why is blame language kept out of incident reports?
options: Blame words are difficult to spell
Because cause-finding belongs to the enquiry; the report's job is verified facts, on which blame or learning is later based
questions.explain: Facts first. If reports mix opinion and blame, the enquiry cannot separate what happened from what someone felt.

questions.q: External agencies like police and fire are engaged during a big incident:
options: By any staff member from personal contacts
Through laid-down contacts, coordinated via Operations Control Centre (OCC)/management
questions.explain: Agency help comes through official, laid-down contacts so that response is coordinated and recorded, not random.

questions.q: A late report reaches Operations Control Centre (OCC) two hours after a minor incident. The correct handling is:
options: Accept and record it marked as a late entry, with actual times shown
Back-date it to the incident time quietly
questions.explain: Honesty over neatness: mark it late and record true times. A visibly late entry is a process issue; a back-timed one is falsification.

questions.q: Which of these belongs in an incident report?
options: 'Probably the motor is burnt, in my opinion'
'The driver is careless and always late'
'At 14:05, Train 204 stopped at km 12.4; driver reported loss of traction; section protected at 14:07'
questions.explain: Times, place, facts, action taken — that is a report. Opinions, guesses and punishment demands are not.

questions.q: The purpose of preserving Closed-Circuit Television (CCTV) and recordings after an incident is to:
options: Punish as many staff as possible
Allow a fair, fact-based reconstruction of what actually happened
questions.explain: Evidence protects the innocent and identifies the real cause. Without it, enquiries run on memory and opinion.

questions.q: When should the first voice report of an incident reach Operations Control Centre (OCC)?
options: Immediately, as soon as the person at site can safely make it
After the written report is ready
questions.explain: Immediately. Every minute of delay is a minute Operations Control Centre (OCC) cannot protect the section or send help.

questions.q: A supervisor learns that a near-miss at his station was never reported by the staff involved. The correct response is:
options: Ignore it, no harm was done
Ensure it is reported and recorded now, marked with its actual reporting time
Delete the Closed-Circuit Television (CCTV) to close the matter
questions.explain: Near-misses must be reported — they are free lessons. Record it now, honestly timed, so the system can learn.

questions.q: During a major incident, who keeps the master log of events and decisions?
options: Operations Control Centre (OCC)/control, as the single master record
The driver of the affected train
questions.explain: One master record at Operations Control Centre (OCC) prevents five conflicting versions. Stations keep local notes, but the Operations Control Centre (OCC) log is authoritative.

questions.q: The stand-down message at the end of an emergency should include:
options: The names of staff to be punished
Confirmation that the area is certified safe/normal and which restrictions, if any, continue
questions.explain: Stand-down must state the certified position clearly — what is normal again and what is still restricted — so nobody guesses.

questions.q: Why are late, altered or casual reports themselves treated as a safety failure?
options: Because decisions, enquiries and learning all depend on the record — a bad record can hide the real cause and repeat the incident
questions.explain: Reporting discipline is safety discipline. A corrupted record defeats protection, enquiry and prevention together.

questions.q: A train crew finishes handling a medical emergency and the passenger is handed over. To close the loop correctly they must:
options: Report completion to Operations Control Centre (OCC) and ensure the incident is documented with times and actions
Announce the passenger's medical details to everyone
Wait for the passenger to thank them
questions.explain: Report completion back to Operations Control Centre (OCC) and document it. The loop closes with a report, not with silence.

questions.q: During a major incident, a television reporter calls the station office for details. Staff should:
options: Give their personal view of the cause
Refer the query to the authorised spokesperson / public relations channel and give out no facts or opinions themselves
Refuse to say even whether trains are running
questions.explain: One authorised voice speaks to the media. Unauthorised comments create wrong news, panic and legal trouble — while passenger-facing service information still continues normally.

questions.q: An escalation contact matrix (a ready list kept at the control desk) is useful because it fixes in advance:
options: The duty rosters for next month
Which authority is to be called for which type and size of incident, with current phone numbers — so nobody searches for contacts mid-emergency
questions.explain: Escalation fails most often at 'whom do I call now?' A tested, updated matrix turns that into a ten-second lookup during the worst minutes.

questions.q: Before a damaged section is handed back for normal working, the departments involved record agreement through:
options: A joint inspection note — signed by the responsible departments — recording what was checked, what was repaired and any restriction that continues
A photograph shared on social media
questions.explain: The joint note is the document that says 'we have all seen it and accept it back'. Signatures make responsibility clear if questions come later.

questions.q: Voice recordings and Closed-Circuit Television (CCTV) footage of an incident are handed over for investigation. Good evidence practice requires:
options: Labelling, sealing and recording every handover (chain of custody) so the evidence is provably untouched
Keeping a copy on a personal phone
questions.explain: Evidence that cannot prove it is untouched loses its value. The chain-of-custody record — who held it, when, and in what condition — is what makes recordings believable.

questions.q: At the end of each shift, the control organisation compiles a daily occurrence report. Its main purpose is:
options: Giving management one factual summary of the day's incidents, failures and pending matters so patterns, pending repairs and risks are visible at a glance
questions.explain: Individual reports tell single stories; the daily summary shows the whole day. Repeated small failures visible in it are tomorrow's big incident, caught early.
